signals.title: Why Stripe is not what you need to charge for your AI product (kind of)
signals.summary: Like everyone else, you build a product and need to charge your customers. Your first instinct is to go to Stripe. Stripe is the GOAT, so of course you'll use it. This is true and untrue, let's say you're building an AI product. You probably won't charge your customers a flat monthly fee that covers all usage as they have a really different cost for your business depending on how they use your product. Instead, you might want to have pricing based on usage. Sounds good. Stripe covers that, case closed... Well, yes and no. There are two types of usage-based billing. One lets customers use the product and pay later, which exposes your business to unpaid bills, and we don't want that... The other uses credits purchased up front. Credits are what most businesses are moving toward nowadays. They give security on both sides, for the business and the customer. They also show you not only how your customers use your product but more importantly how they spend in your product. So you're sold on credits, great, let's set them up in Stripe. signals.summary: arXiv:2611.33497v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically optimises evidence selection for semantic relevance, whereas compliance-sensitive long-form generation also requires evidence supporting explicit structural obligations. Semantically relevant retrieval may therefore omit information needed for mandatory downstream clauses. We propose Constraint-Aligned RAG (CA-RAG), a retrieval-conditioning framework that augments section-specific queries with ontology-derived structural constraints and policy-grounded knowledge-graph relations before evidence selection. Retrieval-only evaluation with manually annotated evidence shows consistent improvements across retrieval budgets. At $k=6$, CA-RAG increases Precision@$k$ from $0.5268$ to $0.5692$, pooled Recall@$k$ from $0.5402$ to $0.5950$, and F1@$k$ from $0.5389$ to $0.5672$ over standard RAG. Generation experiments further show improvements in compliance and reliability in several model--domain settings, while generation-only constraints achieve higher clause coverage but lower overall compliance and reliability. signals.title: Learning to Reason in Real-Time
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.33513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents that operate in the real world must reason correctly and on-time, yet they currently do not account for how time should alter their reasoning. Modern agents learn to do tasks in environments that are entirely synchronous: where the world waits for the agent to act before changing. A real-time environment, by contrast, changes independent of the agent. Existing approaches try to bridge this gap by imposing a ratio of thinking to acting. However, for an agent to succeed in real-time it must learn to act quickly when delay is costly and to reason longer when the benefit outweighs the missed opportunities. To this end, we introduce real-time reasoning training (RRT) as the class of training techniques for real-time reasoning agents. We develop three standard RRT techniques: (1) using real-time data, (2) decoupling acting and observing, and (3) curriculum learning in time. Together, these simple techniques substantially outperform strong baselines.
